title: With great joy (Luke 24:50–53)
hookLine: he blesses them as he's carried up, and they return with great joy
tomorrow: In the beginning was the Word

cards: How do you say goodbye to someone you won't see again in this life? An airport curb, a hospital bed, a last visit with a grandparent.
A goodbye like that can empty a person out: the quiet drive home, the minutes sitting in the car before going inside. Luke's Gospel ends with a goodbye too. But the people in it don't go home quiet.
They go home, of all things, with joy.

teach.h: HE LIFTS HIS HANDS AND BLESSES.
teach.b: Here's the ending, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he led them out as far as Bethania: and lifting up his hands, he blessed them." While he is blessing them, he is parted from them and carried up to heaven.
His last gesture in this Gospel is a blessing, hands lifted the way a priest blesses, still doing it as he goes.
Then: "And they adoring went back into Jerusalem with great joy." They had every reason for grief. Why joy?
He gave them understanding. He promised power from on high. And he left blessing them, so the last thing they saw was not his absence but his care.

teach.h: IT ENDS WHERE IT BEGAN, THE TEMPLE.
teach.b: Now look where Luke ends: in the temple, always praising and blessing God. Where did this Gospel begin, about fifty days ago on this path?
In the temple, with an old priest named Zachary, struck silent at the altar, unable to speak to the people waiting outside.
Some readers see a frame: a priest who couldn't speak to the people at the start, and at the end, hands lifted in blessing and people blessing God in return.
Between them, the whole Gospel: the angel and Mary, the manger, the boy in the temple, the sermon at Nazareth, the lost and found, the cross, the road to Emmaus.
Joy runs through it, from the angel's good tidings of great joy at Bethlehem to this last line.
And Luke wrote a second volume, the Acts of the Apostles, which tells the ascension again, more fully, with forty days and a cloud. Catholics celebrate that day as the Ascension of the Lord.

how: Catholics celebrate the Ascension of the Lord forty days after Easter (moved to the following Sunday in many dioceses), and the Mass ends each time with the priest blessing the people before they are sent out.

practice: Picture someone you said goodbye to today, even an ordinary goodbye, a kid at school drop-off, a coworker leaving, a parent on the phone, going on with their evening.

Wish them good on purpose: their sleep, their worries, their tomorrow, so the last thing you hold tonight is care, not absence. If you pray, ask God to bless them by name; if you don't, just send them the wish.

wordCard.voice: Bethania. Where Jesus led his disciples, lifted his hands to bless them, and was carried up to heaven, the last page of Luke's story. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: great joy, the same words the angel uses at Bethlehem (Luke 2:10) and Luke's last note (24:52).
